description:
We are Team Athena, a group of future engineers who are passionate about Aerospace and the future of space exploration. 

Somos Team Athena, un grupo de futuros ingenieros apasionados por la industria aeroespacial y el futuro de la exploración espacial.
summary:
B.O.M.S. (Base On Mars) is a browser game that works as a mission simulator for junior astronauts aged 7 to 12. Team Athena built it in Godot 4. Players live the whole mission. First they launch, travel to Mars and land the ship in a short minigame. Then they command a crew of four astronauts who must build a base in Jezero Crater and keep it running. To survive, kids mine real Martian resources (regolith, water ice, hematite, silica, gypsum), turn them into materials and build technologies based on real NASA projects:

-an oxygen generator based on MOXIE
-a Veggie-style greenhouse
-an expandable habitat like BEAM
-3D-printed structures
-solar panels
-a Kilopower-type nuclear reactor

The crew must also be protected from solar storms, dust storms, radiation and toxic perchlorates, while players manage food, water, health and rest. Every game mechanic comes from a real fact, and 21 illustrated posters inside the ship explain the science with their sources. B.O.M.S. turns NASA open data into decisions children can understand, so they learn by playing and get interested in space science and engineering.
details:
What it does and how it works

B.O.M.S. (Base On Mars) is a pixel-art game about exploring and managing a base on Mars. It runs in any web browser with nothing to install. The mission comes in four parts: a rocket launch with sound effects, the trip to Mars, a landing minigame scored with stars, and finally the Mars base. The game starts inside the landed ship, which is also the crew’s first shelter. From there, players go out to explore a large map covered by fog and use a mineral scanner to find hidden deposits. They collect regolith, water ice, hematite, silica, gypsum and meteorites, and turn them into bricks, sulfur concrete, glass, metal and other materials. With those materials they build a habitat, an oxygen generator, a workshop, a greenhouse, a laboratory, a solar field, a communications antenna and a radiation wall. Each solar panel has to be made and installed one at a time. The nuclear reactor arrives with the initial cargo, as it would on a real mission. Three AI-controlled astronauts work, eat, sleep, get sick and look for shelter on their own, so the player has to plan for the whole crew and not only for themselves.

Space weather is the core challenge. Solar storms are modeled on events recorded in NASA’s DONKI database, and their radiation doses use the measurements from Curiosity’s RAD instrument. Dust storms cut solar power, as happened to InSight and Opportunity, and a countdown warning gives players time to get everyone to shelter. Astronauts can become ill from radiation or perchlorate dust and need the infirmary, and they also need food, water, exercise and sleep. Short minigames turn daily tasks into play, such as pedaling the exercise bike, growing plants, cleaning the solar panels and focusing the microscope. Inside the ship, 21 illustrated posters teach real facts, each with its source. They cover topics like the length of a Martian day, the 4 to 24 minute delay of messages between Earth and Mars, the oxygen MOXIE made on Mars, the 72 flights of the Ingenuity helicopter and the pizza night astronauts once had on the Space Station.

Benefits and intended impact

Children learn how hard it really is to live on Mars by making decisions, not by memorizing facts. They practice planning, resource management and thinking ahead, and they find out what real NASA missions have discovered. The game can be played in English or Spanish and the language can be changed at any moment, which makes it useful for children in Mexico and Latin America who rarely get space science material in their own language. Because it runs in a browser, teachers can use it in class on any school computer.

Tools and technologies

We built the game with Godot Engine 4, a free and open-source engine, and wrote it in GDScript. It uses the Compatibility renderer and a single-threaded web export so it works on ordinary computers, and it is hosted on itch.io. Most of the pixel art is drawn in code, and the building art designed by our team was converted to the same pixel scale with Python and Pillow so every element shares one style. The retro sound effects are also generated in code. We used Claude, an AI assistant made by Anthropic, to help write code, create pixel art and look for sources. The team made all design decisions and checked every fact used in the game.

Creativity

B.O.M.S. mixes the calm feel of farming games with the real problems of a space mission. Each building is based on a real concept: the laboratory on the Columbus and Destiny modules, the workshop on NASA’s 3D-Printed Habitat Challenge, and the reactor on Kilopower. We designed the difficulty to feel calm and fun while still being dangerous enough to teach why every decision matters.

Factors we considered

We kept the target age in mind at all times, so the controls are simple, texts are short and every window has icons and images. Scientific accuracy was just as important, so every number in the game has a source. We tuned the difficulty to be challenging without becoming frustrating, made sure the game works in a browser on ordinary school computers, and kept one consistent art style across the whole game.
